title: When Everyone Is Responsible, Who's Accountable?
author: Kurt Mueller
source: Rookie to Pro: The Hidden Side of Leadership (kurtmueller.substack.com), October 30, 2026
summary: Kurt Mueller addresses the familiar situation in which a deliverable is late, several people were involved, and nobody can say who was accountable. He argues that leaders who lack authority over reporting lines can still shape how accountability is established, and he offers three moves. First, diagnose the gap by asking whether ownership, decision authority or delivery confirmation is missing, since a missed deadline often looks like poor performance when the real cause is unclear ownership or an unresolved decision. Second, separate decision authority from delivery responsibility and ask a neutral question that moves the conversation from blame to agreement. Third, make the commitment explicit by confirming owner, deliverable, deadline and follow-up, and by asking each person to confirm. A short case about a recurring handoff delay between two departments shows that the fix was assigning someone to confirm the final handoff, not a reorganization. His closing point is that accountability exists only when people understand, accept and follow through on commitments.
points: Diagnose before blaming: check whether ownership, decision authority or delivery confirmation is the missing piece.
Being involved in work is not the same as being accountable for its completion; name one coordinator who confirms decisions and delivers the result.
Frame the question as 'who has authority to decide and who will be accountable for delivery' to move from blame to a workable agreement.
Confirm four essentials aloud and in writing: owner, deliverable, deadline and follow-up.
Making accountability visible, such as designating who confirms the final handoff, can fix recurring failures without any reorganization.
quotes: When accountability is unclear, work gets delayed, decisions are avoided, and frustration grows. Worse yet, everyone may be working hard while important commitments go unfulfilled.
A missed deadline may appear to be a performance problem when the real issue is an unresolved decision or unclear ownership.
Being involved in the work is not the same as being accountable for its completion.
This question shifts the conversation away from assigning blame and toward establishing a workable agreement.
Verbal agreement usually isn’t enough. Accountability becomes meaningful when expectations are specific and visible.
The solution didn’t require a reorganization or additional authority. It required making accountability visible.
Accountability isn’t established simply by telling people they’re responsible. It’s established when people clearly understand, accept, and follow through on their commitments.
